## What happened

HW1 ended on a puzzle. The air across the Los Angeles basin was worse in
early December than in the week of the fires, on days when nothing was
burning anywhere in the state. And the fire's own smoke, from two fires
that burned for three weeks, was gone from the monitors within days.

Both fires were driven by the
[Santa Ana winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Ana_winds), a dry
wind that blows from the desert, over the mountains, and out to sea. On
the night of 7 January 2025 it gusted past 100 km/h. The rest of the
winter the basin's air mostly sat still, and Los Angeles in winter is
famous for inversions: a lid of warm air that traps whatever is emitted
underneath it.

Many of the sites that measure PM2.5 also measure wind, and EPA publishes
that record too, every day, for every instrument. This assignment puts
the two records side by side and asks: **was it the wind?**

## What you produce

One figure, and a note.

It is your HW1 figure with one new panel. Panel **A** is unchanged.
Panel **B** is new: wind speed across the wind monitors, each day,
summarised exactly the way panel A summarises PM2.5. Panel **C** is
HW1's heat map, unchanged.

![Target figure](https://arielortizbobea.github.io/assets/data/hw2_target.png)

Study it before you write a line. The network's worst days, in early
December and at New Year, are days when the wind across the basin
averaged under 5 km/h. The fire week is the one stretch where the basin
was windy and dirty at the same time.

**The note** is a short file, `CHANGES.md`, that says what you changed
from your HW1 project and why, what you checked, and how you used AI.
The format is below.

**The wind data.** One file, cut from EPA's
[pre-generated annual files](https://aqs.epa.gov/aqsweb/airdata/download_files.html)
(`daily_WIND_2024.zip` and `daily_WIND_2025.zip`) to the same area and
window as HW1's file: every wind monitor within 150 km of the Eaton Fire,
1 December 2024 to 28 February 2025. The columns are exactly as EPA
ships them.

> <https://arielortizbobea.github.io/assets/data/epa_wind_la_fires_2024_2025.csv>

6,702 rows, 38 sites, 2.2 MB. Two parameters share the file:
`Parameter Code` **61103** is wind speed, **61104** is wind direction.
This assignment uses speed; direction waits for HW3.

The layout is not the one HW1's file used. EPA's download tool does not
offer wind, so this file comes from a different EPA product with its own
conventions:

| what | HW1's PM2.5 file | this file |
|:--|:--|:--|
| site | `Site ID`, one column, `060371103` | three columns: `State Code` `06`, `County Code` `037`, `Site Num` `1103` |
| instrument | `POC` | `POC` |
| date | `Date`, `01/07/2025` | `Date Local`, `2025-01-07` |
| the value | `Daily Mean PM2.5 Concentration` | `Arithmetic Mean`, the day's average |
| units | µg/m³ | `Units of Measure` says **Knots**; 1 knot is 1.852 km/h |
| the fastest hour | | `1st Max Value`, `1st Max Hour` |

All three site columns are labels with leading zeros, so all three need
protecting at read time, the way `Site ID` did in HW1.

**The PM2.5 data** is HW1's file, at the same address:

> <https://arielortizbobea.github.io/assets/data/epa_pm25_la_fires_2024_2025.csv>

## The rules the figures follow

1. **Everything HW1's figure encoded still holds:** the window, what a
   monitor is, the 60-of-90-days rule, distance from the Eaton Fire, the
   row order, EPA's six colours, the two summaries in panel A, the one
   red line at 7 January.
2. **A wind monitor is a site plus a `POC`.** Build the key from the
   three site columns and the POC. It is unique on any given day within
   parameter 61103, and your script checks that it is. That test is worth
   more than it looks: drop the `61103` filter and the file still holds a
   speed row and a direction row for the same instrument on the same day,
   so the test stops the script.
3. **Keep the wind speed rows only**, parameter `61103`.
4. **Convert knots to km/h**, multiplying by 1.852. The constant lives
   in the parameters block, with its name.
5. **Keep wind monitors that reported at least 60 of the 90 days**, the
   same rule as for PM2.5.
6. **Panel B:** for each day, the mean across the wind monitors that
   reported, and the 10th and 90th percentile of those same readings.
   Axis from 0 to 30 km/h. Same lines, same colours, same key as panel A.
7. **Layout:** three rows, heights in the ratio 1 : 0.75 : 2.6, one
   shared set of margins so the three x axes line up. The red line runs
   from the top of A to the bottom of C.
8. **Output:** `figures/hw2_target.png`, 183 × 270 mm, 300 dpi. The page
   is taller than HW1's so the heat map keeps its row height.

**Panels A and B are the same drawing on two grids.** Write it once as a

## Checking as you go

Panel B draws whether or not the numbers behind it are right. Wind speed
left in knots gives you the same shape, the same 7 January peak, a line
about half as high, and no error anywhere. Session 10 covered the
answer: the script says what it expects and stops when the data
disagrees.

Put a check where this week's data can go wrong, and write it so that it
could actually fail. The size of the wind numbers is the one that matters
most. The tips below give you the scale: an ordinary day across the
network reads 3 to 5 km/h and the Santa Ana reads 13.

```r
  # after the wind grid is built, in code/1_get_clean_data.R
  daily <- apply(grid_wind, 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  stopifnot(median(daily) > 3,    # it is 2.7 if the conversion never ran
            median(daily) < 8)    # it is 9.1 if it ran twice
```

In km/h that median is 4.9 and the script carries on. Both bounds can
fail on a mistake you could actually make, which is what makes the line
worth writing. It also catches a parameter code mistyped as `61104`,
where the median comes out above 300.

Rule 2's key test is the other one. It costs one line and it stops the
script if the `61103` filter never ran. What it cannot see is a filter
that ran on the wrong code, which is why the two checks are worth having
together.

**A check that cannot fail earns nothing.** `max(grid_wind) < 150`
passes on knots and on km/h alike, because the fastest cell in this file
is 38 km/h. `stopifnot(nrow(w) == 6702)` passes today, says nothing
about whether what you did to the rows was right, and breaks the week EPA
regenerates the file.

Printing the number of rows after each step that can drop rows, and the
number of monitors before and after the 60-of-90 rule, is worth doing
and worth quoting in `CHANGES.md`. The check the rubric looks for is one
that stops.

## The note

`CHANGES.md`, at the project root, half a page at most, written in your
own words:

```
# What changed from HW1

Base: my own HW1 submission.

## Files and folders
- ...what you renamed, moved, split or added, and why...

## code/1_get_clean_data.R
- ...one bullet per change, with the reason...

## code/2_plot_figure.R
- ...

## Layout
- ...page size, the three rows and their heights, margins, what you had
  to change so the panels still line up and the labels still fit...

## What I fixed from my HW1
- ...anything your feedback flagged, and what you did about it...

## What I checked
- ...one line per check: where it sits, and what it would have caught...

## AI disclosure
- Tools: which ones, by name
- Used for: what you asked them to do
- Checked: what you verified, and how
```

Prose, not a diff. "Moved the scripts into `code/` so the project
matches the layout the assignment asks for" is a sentence; a list of
changed line numbers is not.

The grader reads the note first, then compares your HW2 code with your
HW1 code. Every change in the code should be in the note, and nothing in
the note should be missing from the code.

**Write the note yourself.** A chatbot will write a flawless one from a
diff in ten seconds. The point of the note is that *you* read the change.
Ask AI to explain a line you changed, by all means. The note describes
what you did, in your words.

## Tips

**Three rows shrink your text.** `layout()` with three or more rows
quietly sets `par("cex")` to 0.66, so every label and every margin is a
third smaller than in HW1 and the site names no longer fit. Put
`par(cex = 1)` right after `layout()`.

**The red line has further to go.** Your HW1 geometry assumed one panel
above the heat map. Now there are two. Derive the top of panel A from the
three layout heights rather than from the single ratio 2.6.

**What "resultant" means.** EPA's daily wind speed is a *vector* average
over the 24 hours: a day when the wind blows one way in the morning and
back in the afternoon averages close to zero. That is why an ordinary day
reads 3 to 5 km/h and the Santa Ana reads 13. It is the right number for
this question, because it measures how far the day's air actually moved.

**The site ID in three pieces.** `paste0()` of the three columns gives
HW1's `Site ID`. You do not need it this week, but it is how HW3 will
match a wind monitor to a PM2.5 monitor at the same site.

**Restart and source before you submit.** Session > Restart R, then
`source("code/run_everything.R")`. It must run top to bottom, with both
files absent from `data/`, and write the figure.

## How to submit

Your repository is **`hw2-<your github username>`**, inside the course
organization. It is already there, and your HW1 submission is already in
it. Find it at <https://github.com/aem6850-cornell> or in the
repositories list on your GitHub home page.

This is the first assignment you submit with git. Three commands, from
[session 7](https://arielortizbobea.github.io/aem6850/fall-2026/sessions/07-git.html):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/aem6850-cornell/hw2-<your username>.git
# ... work, as often as you like ...
git add -A
git commit -m "what you changed"
git push
```

**Commit in the order you work.** The grader reads `git log` first and
grades the last commit pushed before the deadline. A reasonable
sequence:

1. Repair your HW1 figure against the HW1 target. Nothing about wind
   yet; the project still draws one figure and still runs.
2. Move the project into the layout above, if it is not already there,
   and source it from a restarted session.
3. Add the wind file to `code/1_get_clean_data.R`: the URL, the three
   character columns, the speed rows, the conversion, the checks. The
   figure does not change yet.
4. Turn panel A's drawing into a function and call it once for panel A.
   The figure is identical to the previous commit's.
5. Add panel B by calling the same function on the wind grid, with the
   three-row layout and the longer red line.

Then `CHANGES.md`, written last, from the history you already have.
Messages like "Repair the percentile lines in panel A" and "Add wind to
script 1, with the unit and key checks". The number of commits is yours,
and a step that took two tries is two commits. What is graded is that
the repair, the data and the drawing are separable and in a sensible
order, and that each message names what changed. If your HW1 figure
already matched its target, skip step 1 and say so in the note. The
whole assignment arriving as one commit costs you under the last
dimension even when everything in it is right. If a push problem is what
kept you to one commit, say so on the day and it is not counted against
you. RStudio's Git pane and VS Code do the same three steps with
buttons; session 7 shows all three ways.

**What has to be in that final commit:**

- `code/1_get_clean_data.R`
- `code/2_plot_figure.R`
- `code/run_everything.R`
- `CHANGES.md`

Leave `data/` and `data_clean/` out; the `.gitignore` in your repo
already does that for you. You do not need to commit the figures either.
The grader clones your repo fresh, runs `code/run_everything.R`, which
downloads both CSVs and rebuilds everything, and grades the figures your
code draws.

**Before you push for the last time:** Session > Restart R, then
`source("code/run_everything.R")`. If it writes the figure with no
errors, you are done.

**Stuck on git?** Office hours, or ask in the course channel. Do not let
a push problem cost you the deadline: a repo that will not push is a
problem to raise on the day, not the night before.

## AI on this one

Recommended, from here on. The things it is good at this week, in the
chat tier:

- **Explain the wind file.** Paste the header line and the first three
  rows and ask what each column is. Then check the answer against EPA's
  [file format page](https://aqs.epa.gov/aqsweb/airdata/FileFormats.html).
- **Turn panel A into a function.** Paste your panel A code and ask for a
  function that draws it for any grid. Read every line it gives back
  against the code you pasted.
- **Debug the shrinking text.** Describe what you see. Ask why. Then check
  the reason in `?layout`.
- **Draft the README.** It can write prose from your code. Your note it
  cannot write, see above.
- **Ask where it could go wrong quietly.** Give it the wind file's header
  and the steps your script takes, and ask which mistakes would still
  draw a figure. Then ask for one line that would catch each. Read them
  before you keep any: several will pass on this file whatever you did,
  and one of them will quietly drop rows to make the data agree. Keep the
  ones that can fail, and say in the disclosure which you asked for and
  which you wrote.

Three rules, from the syllabus and session 8. **Ask for the script, not
the answer:** a number a chatbot typed is not a result. **Verify one
claim per conversation**, on principle, and say which in the note.
**Disclose.** The disclosure block in your note lists the tools, what you
used them for, and what you checked. Disclosed use is never penalised.
Undisclosed use is misrepresentation under the syllabus and is treated as
an integrity violation.

## Rubric

**12 points.** Four dimensions, three points each. The grader clones
your repo into an empty folder, sources `code/run_everything.R` in a
fresh R session, compares the figure with the target, reads the checks
your script makes, and reads your note against your commits, the first
of which is your HW1.

### Replicability (3 points)

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **3** | The code runs start to finish, without any edits, and writes the figure. Paths are relative to the project root. Nothing depends on objects left over from an earlier session. |
| **2** | The code requires one minor edit to run: a stray absolute path, a folder it expected to exist, a `library()` call for something base R already does. |
| **1** | The code requires several edits to run, or runs with errors, or does not produce the figure. |
| **0** | The code does not run. |

### Similarity (3 points)

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **3** | The figure is virtually identical to the target. One has to really pay attention to see any difference. |
| **2** | The figure is similar but has some clear differences from the target: panel B on the wrong scale or missing a summary, the red line stopping short, labels missing. |
| **1** | The figure is clearly different from the target. |
| **0** | No figure. |

Similarity is judged on what the figure encodes, not on pixel-level
matching. Panel C is judged against the HW1 target: if your heat map was wrong in
HW1, repairing it is part of this assignment and you are not scored
against your own version.

### Coding (3 points)

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **3** | The code (1) has clear and logical sections, (2) has a clearly identified parameter section that can be modified to produce slightly different versions of the output, including the new file, the parameter code and the unit conversion, (3) is well annotated, (4) is concise but spacious: one drawing for panels A and B, not two, and (5) checks its own data where this week's data can go wrong, with at least one check that stops the script and that could have failed on a mistake the student could make. |
| **2** | The code has at most one of the following: (1) no clear structure, (2) parameters hard-coded within the core of the script, (3) missing key annotations, (4) too dense or too verbose, (5) no check beyond the one rule 2 already asks for, or only checks that cannot fail: a row count compared with a number taken from the same run, a bound so wide that both the right and the wrong answer pass, a test that the line above ran. |
| **1** | The code has more than one of those. |
| **0** | There is no code, or the code cannot perform the basic steps needed to generate the output. |

### The note and the history (3 points)

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **3** | The repo's first commit is still the one the course made, and your HW2 scripts are that code edited: your object names, your section headers and your comments are still in them. The work arrives in separable commits in a sensible order, each message naming what that commit did. `CHANGES.md` gives every change with its reason, names the files that moved and the layout changes, says for each check what it would have caught, and discloses the tools, the uses and the checks. |
| **2** | One of those falls short: the whole assignment arrives in a single commit, or the messages say only "update", or the order contradicts the note, or a change in the code is missing from the note, or the file and layout changes are glossed over, or the checks are stated vaguely. A push problem you raised on the day is not counted here. |
| **1** | Two or more fall short. Also here, whatever else is true: your HW2 scripts share nothing with the first commit's, not an object name, not a section header, not a comment, so they did not grow out of your HW1. Files you moved from the repo root into `code/` count as moved, not replaced. |
| **0** | No note, or you pushed no commit of your own. Also here: the repo's first commit is no longer the one the course made, because the repository was replaced or the history rewritten. If that first commit holds no R code, because you did not submit HW1 or your HW1 arrived as a zip, say so in the first line of `CHANGES.md`: you have nothing to build on, and this dimension is then scored on your commits and your note alone. |
